title: GEO for Mobile Apps: How to Improve Your Visibility in AI Search
summary: Learn how to audit your app's store listing, website, reviews, and external coverage to improve its visibility in AI search.
body_markdown:
More people now find apps by asking an AI assistant instead of searching for it on an app store. **[58% of US adults](https://www.apptweak.com/en/aso-blog/ai-app-discovery-survey)** use an AI search engine to find or choose a new app or game. Many will even still check the app store to confirm and download an AI recommended app.


AI now matches Google and social media as the place people first hear about a new download. Whether your app shows up in those answers depends on what’s written about it publicly and whether that information is clear, accurate, and easy to trust.


However, the useful question isn’t how to rank or get mentioned in an AI answer. It’s whether the public information about your app clearly explains what it does, who it’s for, and why someone should trust what it says.


In a recent episode of Tenjin ROI 101 podcast, An Nayal, founder of the couples app Flamme explains how he grew his app with organic social and GEO, and why he treats AI assistants as a discovery route. This guide turns his advice into a practical audit, so that AI systems learn about your app: app store listings, your website, user reviews, and third-party coverage.


## **What Is GEO for Mobile Apps?**


GEO (generative engine optimization) is the process of improving and optimizing how your brand appears in AI-generated answers from tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini, and Google’s AI Overviews. In practice, that means writing accurate, specific information about your app that’s easy for tools to find, understand and trust.


When you check how your app shows up, note the different outcomes, since each one says something different about your approach:


**Outcome** **Display** **Meaning**


Mention The answer names your app The AI knows that your app exists, but it may not understand when or where it fits


Recommendation The answer suggests your app for a need The AI connects your app to a specific problem


Citation The answer links to a page as a source The page the AI relied on for the response


A mention without a recommendation is a weak result.
And a citation tells you which page the AI used.


For An, getting any of these outcomes became a priority because of the new way that people look for apps.


> *People go and ask GPT for an app. They ask a lot for an app.*


He’s not alone in noticing this shift. According to an AppTweak survey with 1,000 adults based in the United States, around 10% said they first heard about their most recent app download from an AI assistant. That’s close to the share as Google Search (10.7%) and social media (10.4%). But, this discovery trend is something you should test for your app category. Our guide to **measuring your app’s visibility in AI search** shows how.


## **How Does GEO Relate to SEO and ASO?**


The O in GEO, SEO, and ASO all stand for the same thing: optimization. All three schools try to get users to discover your app and products. They also help the right person to understand your app then find your app. What changes most between them is where that discovery happens. It could be an app store, a search results page, or in an AI chat. They overlap more than they compete with each other and a clear website and store listing support all of them.


**ASO** **SEO** **GEO**


Where discovery happens App Store and Google Play search Web search results AI-gene


rated answers and recommendations


What you work on Store listing, keywords, screenshots, ratings Website content, technical health, links Accurate and clear, public information about your app


Main signal to watch Store impressions and listing conversion Rankings, clicks, organic traffic Mentions, recommendations, and citations in sampled answers


For Google, there is no separate guide. Google’s guidance states that SEO best practices still **[remain relevant for AI overviews and AI mode](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)** , and that no additional requirements or special optimizations are needed. Furthermore, the optimization guide adds that these features are built on Google’s core search systems.


But, other AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity, use their own retrieval and sources and these algorithms change often. The safest strategy is the one that works everywhere and retains accuracy, usefulness, and accessible information about your app.


The fundamentals of optimization for different channels overlap. SEO focuses on a high position in a list of links. GEO aims for accurate mentions, recommendations, or citations inside an answer. An sees teams missing this distinction often, treating GEO as SEO with a new name:


*One of the biggest misconceptions and mistakes we see people make is they confuse GEO, AEO with SEO, right?*


## **Where to Audit Your App’s Public Information**


Your app visibility audit only asks one question, anywhere it goes: can an AI system read this page and only this page, would it describe my app well? Work through them in order, starting with the one that you can control the most.


### **1. App Store and Google Play Listings**


Your store listing is often the most authoritative public description of your app. Check that it states:


- **Audience:** who the app is for, in plain words
- **Problem:** the job the app does for them
- **Distinctive features:** what’s different, described specifically
- **Platform support:** iOS, Android, web, or wearables
- **Pricing model:** free, freemium, subscription, and trial length


An goes a step further and recommends answering the questions people ask AI assistants directly in the listing:


> *If a user is going to be asking, “What is an app that can help my relationship?” you should have that question as a part of your App Store listing.*


It’s a useful habit to answer the questions and write in detail about the topics that your user already asks about. Just don’t expect an exact phrase match to unlock a mention or recommendation. It doesn’t work that way, there are many other moving parts involved.


An also sees your app store listing as more than just an asset. As he puts it:


> *Your store listing is now an SEO page for an AI engine.*


Store listings are public and AI assistants with web search can easily read them. So, if your pricing is out of date or your copy is misaligned or vague, it will know and pick it up.


One thing An advises against is naming your app after the keyword you want to be ranked or found for. His team has tested it and the name ended up being too generic to stand out. As a result, he recommends a name built for consumers and for your brand:


> *Every time you name the product just for GEO or SEO purposes, it becomes too common, right?*


### **2. App Website**


Many apps make the mistake of relying on their app store page alone. Why not go the extra mile and also create a website where you can answer more questions and have another owned resource to talk about it?


*So I believe a website has two-sided value. One, it is great for SEO, GEO, but it’s also great when people are actually looking for you.*


A useful app website usually includes:


- One clear main app page that says what the app does, who it’s for, which platforms it supports, and what it costs
- Sections or pages for specific use cases and audiences
- Accurate pricing and availability, updated when they change
- An FAQ that answers real pre-install questions
- Release notes with substance when features change
- Important facts in HTML text, not only in images or video, and linked from the main page


Here’s an illustrative before-and-after for a fictional app called LinkUp:


Before After


“LinkUp helps you build a better relationship.” “LinkUp is a free iOS and Android app for couples in long-distance relationships. Partners answer one shared question a day, keep a countdown to their next visit, and send short voice notes. Premium costs $4.99 a month.”


The second version gives an AI system facts it can repeat: the audience, the features, the platforms, and the price.


Thinking about posting a comparison page? Keep it simple and honest. From his own experience, An notes that a page where your app wins in every single category doesn’t convince anyone. It’s important to be honest and only claim the top spot where you’ve genuinely earned it.


*So one thing we recommend is: create an honest recommendation where you rank top for the thing you list yourself the top for.*


### **3. Authentic User Reviews**


Your reviews show how authentic users talk about your app, its value, and which questions continue to surface. Use them to:


- Observe the words and language that users keep coming back to when they describe your app, especially if it’s about a problem that it solves
- Find the questions or misconceptions that your website or app store listing hasn’t answered yet
- Update your listing and FAQ to address and answer them


An has noticed that a good, detailed review that explains how the app has helped and who it’s good for goes way further than a short review like “good app.”


> *A review like that is highly likely to rank much higher compared to a more generic review.*


This is his experience, rather than a confirmed point in the algorithm, but it’s also a very good reason to encourage thoughtful reviews.


Moreover, making it easier for happy users to leave a review makes all the difference. It’s also important to reply to the ones that aren’t so positive or raise questions. Keeping it real and authentic is what it’s all about: fake, bought, or incentivized reviews break App Store and Google Play rules and they could also misrepresent your app.


### **4. Relevant Third-Party Coverage**


Your website is where you can make claims and share stories about your app. A comparison article, a review, a publication, or community thread is someone else’s evaluation. AI answers often draw on both, and outside sources carry a different kind of weight.


The pages you own still matter, as long as they are honest. But in An’s view, they weren’t meant to carry the whole weight. External validation counts too.


Start with the sources that AI assistants already use for your target prompts.


- Run your prompts and list the third-party URLs that appear as citations
- Check whether those pages mention your app, and whether they describe it accurately
- Where a correction or an inclusion is genuinely relevant, contact the author with evidence, such as a feature list, pricing, or a demo account
- Join communities where your audience asks questions, and say that you’re the founder


You can skip fabricated endorsements, paid link schemes, and mass press releases. They’re unlikely to build lasting AI visibility and could cost you trust in the long run.


## **Prioritize the Gaps You Can Fix**


Once you’ve audited and worked through all the different spaces, you can list each gap you found from your audit and who owns it. Here’s a quick example of what that could look like:


Surface Information gap Evidence Next action Owner


Store listing Old price shown AI answers quote last year’s price Update listing and website pricing Product marketing


Website No page for long-distance couples Category prompts recommend competitors with dedicated pages Add a use-case section Content


Reviews Users unsure about Android support Several recent reviews ask the same question Add a platform FAQ and reply to reviews Support


Third-party coverage App missing from a frequently cited comparison The article is cited in 3 of 10 sampled answers Contact the author with accurate details Founder


If you’re unsure where to begin, An is clear about the first surface:


> *I recommend a good mix of everything, but the store listing comes first.*


Start with your store listing, then work through the rest in this order.


1. Fix anything that is inaccurate.
2. Sharpen your main store listing and main app page.
3. Address use cases you don’t explain yet.
4. Pursue relevant external coverage.
5. Measure again.


For the last step, follow our guide on **how to measure your app’s visibility in AI search.** It covers prompt selection, tracking, and the metrics to compare over time.


## **Where GEO Fits in Your Acquisition Strategy**


Showing up in AI answers helps more people discover your app. What it can’t show is whether those users stick around, pay, or are worth more than users from other channels.


Many AI-assisted installs also look organic: someone reads an answer, then searches the App Store by name. To spot that pattern, watch branded store searches and organic installs alongside your visibility tracking. If you run a “How did you hear about us?” onboarding survey, add “An AI assistant” as an option.

If you also run ChatGPT Ads, Tenjin attributes installs and in-app events from those campaigns, so paid and organic AI traffic can sit side by side in your reports.


If social content is part of how people first hear about your app, read An’s view on **connecting TikTok and AI search** . For the wider picture of finding valuable users, see our[user acquisition strategy guide .](https://tenjin.com/blog/blog-app-user-acquisition-strategy/)


## **Key Takeaways**


- GEO for mobile apps is the work of making sure AI assistants can find, understand, and accurately describe your app.
- GEO overlaps with SEO and ASO. Google says its AI features are rooted in the same core systems as Search.
- Audit four surfaces: your store listings, your website, user reviews, and third-party coverage.
- Fix inaccurate facts first, then clarify, then build coverage, then measure again.


## **Frequently Asked Questions**


****What is GEO for mobile apps?****


GEO (generative engine optimization) for mobile apps is the process of improving how an app is mentioned, recommended, and cited in AI-generated answers. For mobile apps that means making information about the app easy to find across store listings, the app’s website, reviews, and third-party sources.


****Does GEO replace SEO or ASO?****


No. GEO builds on SEO and ASO rather than replacing them. Google says SEO best practices remain relevant for its AI features, and store listings remain a key source of app information for people and AI systems.


****Does my app need a website for AI discovery?****


An app can appear in AI answers without a website, but a website gives AI systems and people a clear source of facts that you control. An, founder of Flamme, recommends one because it supports SEO, GEO, and people searching for the app directly.


****Can I guarantee that ChatGPT will recommend my app?****


No. AI answers vary by prompt, model, settings, and time, and no provider publishes a formula for recommendations. You can improve the accuracy and availability of your app’s information, then track whether visibility changes.


****How can I check whether my app appears in AI answers** ?**


Choose prompts your users would ask, run them several times across the AI assistants your audience uses, and record mentions, recommendations, and citations. Tenjin’s guide to[measuring app visibility in AI search](https://tenjin.com/blog/measure-app-visibility-ai-search/) explains the full process.
